reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents OneCoin as a business opportunity and instructs the account holder to recruit team partners and build a team. It shows sponsor sign-up and member-placement controls alongside purported commissions, earnings, payouts, and KYC requirements for identity documents and a utility bill. The material does not establish that information was submitted, funds were paid, or the claims and privacy assurances were independently verified.

opening.argument: Judge, this is operational guidance accompanied by concrete security and fraud-prevention cautions, not a promise of profit. The presenter recommends changing passwords to prevent fraud and theft, explains that transaction passwords approve transactions, and describes KYC as a measure used to prevent credit-card fraud. Those warnings are inconsistent with portraying the material as a deceptive solicitation: viewers are directed toward account security, identity verification, and asking their bank when uncertain about banking codes. The video does not guarantee earnings or claim that participation is risk-free; it explains settings and procedures while attributing payment and privacy practices to the service itself.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited invite link and placement controls establish that the account can support team activity, but they do not establish deceptive solicitation, a guaranteed return, or that any recruit was actually contacted. Likewise, describing commissions and earnings as a transfer function does not establish that money was deposited or that the claim was verified. The password quote shows an ordinary security procedure, not evidence of fraud.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Security warnings do not answer the central concern: the same tutorial actively facilitates recruiting and arranging people within a team. The material tells users to send a signup link to future team partners and says strategic placement is important. Calling KYC or password changes protective does not show that the underlying opportunity is legitimate, and the payment language still presents commissions and earnings as an expected service outcome.

opening.argument: This is best understood as a technology and account-operations demonstration. Its title identifies a profile-and-settings tutorial, and the narration explicitly introduces a walkthrough of how the back office works before explaining profile settings, password changes, email changes, banking details, and KYC. The sampled interface is consistent with that instructional purpose: it shows settings panels and placement controls, not a completed transaction, a payment receipt, or a demonstrated financial result. Explaining how a platform operates is not the same as certifying every business claim associated with it.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The tutorial format matters. The reference interpretation treats interface explanations as proof of a scam, but the invite and placement sections can simply document available account features. The banking language describes what the system is intended to do, while the cited password instruction is plainly a settings walkthrough. Nothing cited shows a completed recruitment, payout, or false claim.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A tutorial can still promote and operationalize a deceptive scheme. This one does more than describe generic settings: it instructs the account holder to send a signup link to future team partners and recommends building a team through strategic placement. The fact that no completed payout appears does not make those recruitment and commission representations ordinary technical instruction.

opening.argument: The material can be read as documentation for an online business service and its account administration. The visible screens show profile settings, password controls, member-placement options, and bank-detail fields, while the narration explains how to configure them. Crucially, the supplied material does not show a required deposit, a guaranteed return, an actual downline payment, or a completed cash-out. It also does not show a password or identity document being submitted; it only explains fields and procedures. A referral link and a business-team layout may support an ordinary referral or platform function, but they do not by themselves prove fraud.

citations.quote: So OneCoin is able to transfer your comissions and earnings to your bank account.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side identifies features associated with a business platform, but association is not proof of a scam mechanism. A link for signing up a member and left/right placement can be referral administration; the earnings sentence states a purported transfer capability, not a guaranteed return or proof that anyone was paid. The frames show forms and controls, not a completed deposit or cash-out.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The mechanism is not merely a generic referral: the tutorial tells users to recruit team partners, strategically place new members, and build a team, while describing commissions and earnings transferred to a bank account. The absence of a completed payout does not erase the represented income structure. Calling the screens ordinary administration also does not explain why member placement is presented as strategically important.
